The data matches Yahoo's exactly aside from the intraday last value. Checking the 29-session offset, I notice the labeled date seems off by one day—the −6.2% figure they attribute to May 4 actually lines up with May 5's close instead.

Other small discrepancies turn up too: their 3-month volatility figures for S&P and NDX differ slightly from mine, likely due to methodology, and the 12-month NDX run-up differs depending on whether sessions or calendar months are used. The "29 sessions after" NDX figure also seems mislabeled by a date.

Still, my own replication confirms their best-fit correlation claim—peaking around 0.985 in late April to early May 2000, with RMSE best around May 10. The caveat is that this correlation is almost entirely about the overall trend, since the correlation of daily returns is essentially zero, meaning the "near-copy" claim only holds for the broad shape, not the actual day-to-day noise.

Now I want to run a placebo test to see how often a correlation this high (≥0.985) occurs by chance across long-run history, so I'm pulling decades of S&P 500 daily data to compare the current window against every historical 1008-day stretch.

I also need to correct an earlier point: I previously said Nasdaq peaked in May 2026 based on monthly Composite closes, but the daily NDX data shows October 6 as the actual peak—these are different indices and different granularities, so I should flag that distinction when I reply. I'll also quickly check the Composite's daily peak within my placebo script to make sure I'm not conflating the two further.
